stories.headline: Update: Duffy and Mullin to brief media at White House on nationwide FAA ground stop
stories.summary:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin will hold a press conference Friday evening at the White House to discuss the Federal Aviation Administration's decision earlier in the day to impose a nationwide ground stop on all flights. The briefing is the first scheduled public explanation from cabinet-level officials since the stoppage, which was attributed to a rolling frequency outage.

The involvement of both the Transportation and Homeland Security secretaries signals that the administration is treating the episode as more than a routine technical failure. The ground stop halted departures across the country and is among the most sweeping disruptions to U.S. air travel in years, with the potential to affect large numbers of passengers and airline operations.

The story has drawn extensive coverage, with 28 outlets across the political spectrum reporting on it. Officials are expected to address the cause of the outage, how long normal operations will take to resume, and whether any security concerns are involved. Further details on the cause and on any steps to prevent a recurrence are expected from the briefing.

stories.headline: Aide to fugitive Ukrainian ex-PM wounded in Moscow car bombing
stories.summary:
A car bomb in Moscow wounded Sergei Zavorotny, a former press adviser to ex-Ukrainian prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee said. Zavorotny, 72, was behind the wheel of his Toyota when the device exploded. Azarov told Russian television his condition in hospital was "rather critical". Unconfirmed reports said the device was detonated remotely.

Zavorotny worked for Azarov in Kyiv until 2014, when pro-Kremlin president Viktor Yanukovych was toppled and Azarov fled to Russia. A 2020 US Senate report on 2016 election interference described Zavorotny as an SVR officer involved in influence operations. Investigators said they would order medical and explosives examinations.

The blast came a day after a car bomb in St Petersburg killed a Russian military member, reportedly a high-ranking figure in the 6th Guards Air and Air Defence Forces Army. Both attacks are seen as part of a series targeting military and prominent figures linked to the invasion of Ukraine.

Overnight, Ukraine and Russia also traded strikes. Ukrainian authorities said three people, including a 17-year-old, were killed in Odesa and Zaporizhzhia, and that a hospital was hit. Russia said Ukrainian strikes killed four people in Samara and four in Volgograd, and one in Bryansk.

stories.headline: Appeals court rules U.S. wrongly withheld $74 million in New York highway funds over immigrant commercial licenses
stories.summary:
A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Manhattan ruled Friday that the Transportation Department wrongly withheld nearly $74 million in highway money from New York. The court found the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration acted in a manner that was "arbitrary, capricious, or contrary to law" when it penalized the state for not revoking nearly 33,000 questionable commercial driver's licenses issued to immigrants.

The court said New York could not be faulted for failing to cancel licenses when drivers lost legal status, because rules requiring such cancellations were not in place at the time. New York Attorney General Letitia James had sued in April, saying the money was needed for roads and bridges. Gov. Kathy Hochul called the cuts "devastating" and "political payback."

The Transportation Department said it makes no sense for states to let licenses for foreign drivers run years beyond their legal presence in the country, adding, "We've put a stop to the madness to keep the driving public safe." The department says about 26,000 drivers have been removed from the road for failing English proficiency tests and 30,000 licenses were canceled as illegally issued. Immigrants make up about 20% of truck drivers, and immigrant groups argue many drivers are unfairly targeted.

The ruling could shape how the administration uses funding penalties against states over commercial licensing.

stories.headline: Judge signals she may block Trump administration's closure of East Potomac Park golf course
stories.summary:
A federal judge is set to rule this weekend on whether the Trump administration can proceed with closing East Potomac Park and its historic public golf course in Washington. Judge Ana Reyes signaled during a lengthy hearing Friday that she was not poised to allow the closure, at least for now.

Reyes pressed government lawyers on the plan, which is tied to President Trump's wishes to renovate the site. She indicated she could order the park to remain open while the case proceeds.

The ruling is expected to determine whether work on the makeover can begin, and it adds to a series of court challenges over the administration's changes to public landmarks and spaces in the capital.

stories.headline: FAA Halts All Flight Departures Nationwide After 'Rolling Frequency Outage'
stories.summary:
The Federal Aviation Administration halted all flight departures across the United States on Friday afternoon, citing a "rolling frequency outage" affecting facilities that monitor aircraft in the air. The nationwide ground stop disrupted air travel across the country, and the agency has not publicly identified a definitive cause.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday evening that investigators were examining the disruption. He suggested that a telecommunications issue was behind the outage, though officials did not offer further technical detail or say whether any outside interference was suspected.

The event drew coverage from 22 outlets across the political spectrum, reflecting the scale of the disruption to passengers, airlines and air traffic control operations. A nationwide halt of departures is a rare step, typically reserved for serious safety or system failures.

The key open questions are what caused the frequency outage, how quickly normal operations can resume, and whether the telecommunications failure points to vulnerabilities in aviation communications infrastructure. Further statements from the FAA and the Department of Homeland Security are expected as the investigation continues.

stories.headline: All Accounted For After Tanker Strikes Docked River Cruiser in New Orleans
stories.summary:
A tanker lost control and struck the docked American Heritage river cruiser on the Mississippi River in New Orleans around 12:30 p.m. Friday, capsizing the vessel. Officials said everyone aboard was accounted for, and Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry called the outcome "a literal miracle on the Mississippi."

Thirty-two passengers were taken to hospitals, and none had critical injuries, Mayor Helena Moreno said. Two Harbor Police officers were also hospitalized in good condition. Port officials initially reported about 129 passengers plus crew aboard, while Moreno later estimated roughly 180 to 190 people were on the vessel.

Harbor Police responded first, firefighters lowered ladders over the dock, and nearby vessels helped pull people from the water. Police Superintendent Anne Kirkpatrick said a drone already airborne for an unrelated call was redirected to the scene within moments. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham confirmed the search-and-rescue operation had ended.

Investigators are examining an apparent loss of steering aboard the Atlantic Asphalt tanker, though the exact cause is unknown. The National Transportation Safety Board is sending a Go Team, with investigators expected Saturday morning.

stories.headline: Alaska Senate Race Still Uncalled as Peltola Leads Sullivan by 5,800 Votes
stories.summary:
Alaska's Senate race remained uncalled more than a week after Election Day, with former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola leading Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 5,800 votes as officials continue counting absentee ballots.

According to the Associated Press, 88 percent of the vote had been counted. Peltola had 125,157 votes, or 49.2 percent, compared with Sullivan's 119,357, or 47 percent. Two other candidates, Republican Gerald Heikes and independent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., had 5,490 and 4,199 votes respectively.

Election officials are preparing for a ranked-choice tabulation, which could affect the final outcome since no candidate has cleared a majority. The result bears on the final Senate balance after Democratic gains in the midterms, which have already fueled leadership debates within the party.

stories.headline: SpaceX Attempts First Double Catch of Starship Booster and Ship
stories.summary:
SpaceX planned to launch its next Starship test flight Friday from Starbase, Texas, at 4:45 p.m. local time, attempting to catch both parts of the 124-meter rocket with the launch tower's mechanical arms, nicknamed chopsticks.

About six and a half minutes after liftoff, the Super Heavy booster is to return for the first catch attempt. The upper-stage Ship will continue to space, deploy 26 Starlink satellites and complete 14 orbits before a second catch attempt roughly 22.5 hours after launch. SpaceX has caught the booster on three earlier flights, but the Ship, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been caught and has previously splashed down in the ocean.

SpaceX said it would decide on the Ship catch only after assessing the vehicle in space. Success would mark the first full recovery of a rocket that has been to space, a step toward full reusability. Prof Malcolm Macdonald of the Royal Aeronautical Society said full reusability could fundamentally change the economics of accessing space, though one flight would not prove the model.

NASA is watching closely because Starship is central to its Artemis program and an ambitious 2028 Moon landing target. SpaceX went public earlier this year, so shareholders are also following the flight.

stories.headline: Interior Department Plan to Sell Federal Lands Draws Opposition From Both Parties
stories.summary:
The Department of the Interior has laid out plans to sell off federal lands, a proposal that has drawn criticism from Republicans and Democrats alike. Several lawmakers have vowed to block the sale of any land in their states, and the backlash was reported by 12 outlets across the political spectrum.

Sen. Martin Heinrich, a New Mexico Democrat set to chair the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee next year, said he led the successful fight two summers ago against an unprecedented proposal to sell millions of acres of public lands and would do so again. "These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in," he said. Republican Sen. Tim Sheehy of Montana said his office was not consulted and that he will not allow "ONE ACRE" of Montana land to be sold, noting he stopped the sale of lands in the One Big Beautiful Bill last year.

Republican Sen. Steve Daines, Reps. Mike Simpson and Ryan Zinke, who served as Interior Secretary in the first Trump administration, have also confirmed their opposition. Conservation groups including the Sierra Club, the Center for Western Priorities, Nature is Nonpartisan and the Sagebrush Institute are united against the plan. Maya Cohn of Nature is Nonpartisan said selling public lands is "nearly universally unpopular" and noted that land sale provisions were struck from last summer's tax and spending package after sweeping backlash.

The administration has not yet responded in detail to lawmakers' requests for information. Questions remain over how much authority Interior's Bureau of Land Management has under current law to sell land without congressional approval, and lawmakers are expected to press the department for details.

stories.headline: Update: Kremlin Revives Demands for New European Security Architecture After Talks With US Envoys
stories.summary:
Following talks in Moscow between President Vladimir Putin and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the Kremlin said peace requires "a new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace." BBC analysis says this effectively means Moscow wants to reshape Europe's security setup in its favor, potentially the biggest change since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has put back on the table its December 2021 draft treaties with the US and NATO, which would have halted NATO's eastward enlargement, guaranteed that Ukraine and Georgia never join, and rolled back alliance military infrastructure in central and eastern Europe. Western leaders dismissed those demands as an ultimatum, and Russia launched its full-scale invasion two months later. Putin aide Yuri Ushakov also suggested Moscow would "add certain new considerations" to its demands, citing Western efforts to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas called the demands a "trap" meant to shift attention from a ceasefire, saying the priority should be a ceasefire, then a peace agreement, and only then discussion of wider European security. Europe is not currently at the table, though Putin has said Europeans may join the next round of talks. This week's talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US, and the envoys later met Zelenskyy in Dublin.

Overnight, Ukraine and Russia exchanged attacks. Ukrainian authorities said a hospital was hit and three people were killed in Odesa and Zaporizhzhia, while Russia said Ukrainian strikes killed at least nine people in Samara and Volgograd.

stories.headline: Measles Cases Top 5,400 as US Deaths Rise to 10
stories.summary:
The CDC reported 5,412 measles infections across 45 states, 230 more than in the previous week's update. Between 2000 and 2024 the United States averaged 180 cases a year. New deaths were reported Friday in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, bringing the national toll to 10: seven in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin and one in New York.

A decision on whether the United States loses its measles elimination status could come as soon as Friday. The CDC chief has said the agency's response would be unchanged if the status is lost. Kindergarten measles vaccination coverage fell from 95% in 2019 to 92% in 2026, below the roughly 95% level generally needed for herd immunity, and about 300,000 kindergartners entered classrooms this year unvaccinated.

Health officials note that measles is among the most contagious diseases, capable of infecting about 90% of unvaccinated people exposed. About one in five unvaccinated patients is hospitalized, one in 20 children develops pneumonia, and one in 1,000 develops encephalitis. Two MMR doses are 97% effective at preventing infection.

stories.headline: German Parliament Gives Intelligence Services Sweeping New Powers Against Hybrid Threats
stories.summary:
Germany's Bundestag approved a major overhaul of intelligence legislation, voting 309 in favor, 190 against and 71 abstaining. The law gives the BND foreign intelligence service and the BfV domestic service greater powers to counter espionage, terrorism and sabotage. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called it a "reform of the century."

The BND will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage such as paralyzing servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks or weapons supply chains. The BfV will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems when specific threats are identified, including disabling explosives, blocking data flows during cyberattacks and deleting or falsifying malicious data. With prior authorization it may covertly enter homes, and it gains wider digital surveillance powers including monitoring encrypted communications and using AI-supported data analysis and biometric matching.

The government says the reform responds to rising espionage from Russia, China and Iran, citing an August drone with an explosive device found at Leipzig Airport near Ukrainian cargo planes, which authorities attribute to Russia. Dobrindt said Germany is a theater of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers. Left Party security spokeswoman Clara Bunger accused him of creating a new German secret police, which Dobrindt rejected as "madness."

stories.headline: Update: Putin Meets Witkoff and Kushner, Says Europeans Can Join Next Round of Ukraine Talks
stories.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin met U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, for about two hours at the Kremlin on Thursday. Witkoff said afterward that Putin had agreed to let European officials join the next round of Ukraine peace talks, but the Kremlin did not confirm that. The meeting capped a week of diplomacy that produced a large prisoner exchange but no firm commitments toward ending the war.

Putin reiterated sharp differences with Europe over how a settlement should work. Citing European plans to deploy troops in Ukraine once peace is reached, he said that "would mean the continuation of the war. That circle has closed." Witkoff and Kushner then flew to Ireland to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who also stressed that Europeans should be at the table.

Europe's role is a central point of friction. National security advisers from the European Union and five major powers, Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, are expected to represent Europe in the upcoming talks. Moscow has also made fresh demands to discuss European security arrangements as part of any deal, which has exposed divisions within the continent about how to proceed.

The diplomacy comes as Ukraine reports renewed disruptions to the Starshield satellite internet service and as Russian strikes on its power grid force rolling blackouts. Whether Moscow will accept European participation, and on what terms, is the main open question for the next round.

stories.headline: UN Nuclear Watchdog 'Increasingly Concerned' Over Uninspected Iranian Enrichment Site
stories.summary:
The International Atomic Energy Agency said in a new report that it is "increasingly concerned" about a uranium enrichment facility in Isfahan, Iran, that inspectors have not been allowed to visit. The agency said it does not know the plant's exact location or whether it holds nuclear material. Iran announced the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant on June 12, 2025, a day before Israel began striking its nuclear sites, and an inspection that Iran had initially agreed to was cancelled.

Since the current war began, Iran has restricted inspectors' access, preventing the agency from verifying its enriched uranium stockpile. Before the June 2025 strikes, Iran had accumulated an estimated 441 kilograms enriched to 60 percent, close to weapons grade. The IAEA believes much of that material was stored at Isfahan, where above-ground facilities were heavily damaged but the condition of underground sites is unclear.

The agency called the lack of information "a matter of serious proliferation concern" that "needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency." The United States and Israel say their strikes aimed to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons, which Tehran denies seeking, saying its program is for civilian purposes.

The report arrives as the Iran war enters its ninth month and as Tehran weighs leaving the nuclear nonproliferation treaty. President Trump has said the United States does not need a deal with Iran, leaving the fate of the stockpile unresolved.

stories.headline: Update: Bessent Says Commerce 'Has the Pen' on Megaspeed Blacklist, Deepening Pressure on Lutnick
stories.summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Friday CNBC interview that Treasury, the War Department, the U.S. Trade Representative and State agreed to place Megaspeed on a list of companies posing national security concerns, but that the Commerce Department "has the pen." Megaspeed is a Singapore technology company accused of illegally diverting U.S. chips to China. Bessent did not deny reports of tension between him and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

The remarks add to scrutiny of Lutnick after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following reports of affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. Lutnick has agreed to testify before Congress, and the White House is reportedly standing by him despite a view inside the administration that his department delayed action on chip smuggling.

Congressional Democrats, including Sens. Chris Coons and Elizabeth Warren, have asked the administration to preserve documents, and top House Democrats have called for an investigation. Some Republicans have also expressed concern, and Democrats say Lutnick could face hearings or impeachment efforts when they take control of Congress in January. The White House has not signaled any change in his status. China has warned the United States against imposing new chip export controls in response to the scandal.

stories.headline: Update: Sunrise Protesters Arrested at Schumer's Office as Van Hollen Gains Endorsements in Leadership Challenge
stories.summary:
Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota announced Friday that she is backing Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in his challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader. "Minnesotans are demanding change. Democrats need to deliver," she said. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin have also reportedly rejected Schumer's bid, along with several newly elected senators, while Schumer says he has the votes to win.

On Thursday, 54 people from the Sunrise Movement youth climate group were arrested during a sit-in at Schumer's Washington office, according to the group. The protesters are pushing for new leadership and an end to the filibuster. Van Hollen was scheduled to speak in Denver on Friday and has said the American people "called for change." Critics have framed the dispute as a fight over how aggressively to push to end the Iran war and confront corporate power.

Senate Democrats vote by secret ballot on Dec. 1, giving activists nearly three weeks to lobby members. Supporters of Schumer argue that his experience matters as the party prepares to take control of the chamber in January after its midterm sweep. Republicans have pointed to the infighting as evidence of deep divisions within the Democratic Party despite its electoral success.

stories.headline: Update: Democrats Question Jeffries' Leadership After Hegseth Impeachment Vote Failure as He Seeks Speakership
stories.summary:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is facing criticism over a procedural vote this week in which 11 House Democrats were absent. The absences allowed Republican leaders to block Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., from advancing an impeachment resolution against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. Had just seven of the absent Democrats been present, the motion to kill the resolution would have failed, triggering debate and a likely impeachment vote the next day.

The fallout comes as Democrats are projected to win 255 House seats, with 12 races still uncalled, following sweeping gains last week in states including Texas, Mississippi, Kansas and South Carolina. Jeffries is running to become Speaker. Critics from within the party have been vocal. Fred Trump III, a Democrat and nephew of the president, wrote on X that he may have to rethink his support for Jeffries. Sean Vitka of Demand Progress said party leaders had failed to deliver on attendance and handed Republicans a win.

Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., said in a video that she and other Democrats were stuck in traffic. Various reports said they were at a fundraiser less than two miles from the Capitol. Other absences were attributed to medical procedures and family emergencies. Progressive commentators noted that the impeachment effort can be reintroduced and that Democrats will hold a much larger caucus in January.

Republicans have used the episode to question whether Democrats are ready to govern, while Democratic defenders stress that the setback is procedural and temporary. The Speaker contest and the possibility of renewed impeachment efforts are expected to shape the new Congress.

stories.headline: Talarico Urges Democrats to Work With Trump; Trump Signals Possible Military Action Against Cuba
stories.summary:
Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas, told Democrats at the What's Next conference in Denver on Thursday that the party must work with President Trump rather than wait for a new president to take office. He said Democrats should cooperate on economic relief and political reform, and that the goal should be to make Trump's final two years among the most productive of any presidency.

The remarks come after Democrats won back both chambers of Congress in the midterms, and reflect an ongoing debate within the party over how to use its new leverage. Some Democrats favor aggressive oversight and confrontation with the administration, while others argue voters want tangible results on cost-of-living and governance issues.

Separately, Trump signaled in a new interview that he could take military action against Cuba before leaving office in order to topple the island's communist government. The comments add a possible new foreign-policy front while the administration is already engaged in the Iran conflict. Details of any planning were not provided, and no formal move toward action against Cuba has been announced.

stories.headline: African Miss Universe Contestants in Limbo as US Visa Restrictions Bite
stories.summary:
Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other African contestants may miss this year's pageant in Puerto Rico because they have not obtained US visas. The 75th Miss Universe final is scheduled for November 24 at the Jose Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan. Contestants began arriving on November 8 for registration and fittings.

Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions under Presidential Proclamation 10998, effective January 1, 2026. The measures suspend visitor, student, exchange and immigrant visas for nationals of affected countries and restrict other non-immigrant categories. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, a 25-year-old nurse crowned on October 8. Zambia's Miss Universe organization said her situation stemmed from the travel restrictions rather than personal circumstances, and that five other African countries face similar difficulties.

Hall said she spent weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa and noted she is not alone. Miss Universe South Sudan said it was 50/50 whether she would make it. The case illustrates the practical reach of the administration's travel restrictions, which supporters frame as a security measure and critics say sweeps in ordinary travelers.

stories.headline: Neither War Nor Peace in Tigray as Ethiopia's Latest Conflict Leaves Uncertainty
stories.summary:
Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front and Ethiopia's national army, resuming a two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022. Within two weeks, federal forces entered the regional capital Mekelle, as the TPLF carried out what it called a strategic withdrawal from the city and other main towns. Hundreds of people are reported to have died, including dozens killed in drone strikes and air raids.

Ethiopian officials and supporters say the war is effectively over and that the remaining task is clearing TPLF elements. Getachew Reda, a former TPLF official now advising the prime minister, said stabilization should be the priority. Analysts cite the TPLF's loss of popular support, fragmentation, defections and lack of advanced weaponry. TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom rejects the defeat narrative, saying the group deliberately drew the army deeper into Tigray to fight on favorable terrain.

Residents describe an uncertain situation. Salon owner Firut Me'ar said the economy is stalled and people cannot afford basics. A Mekelle University scholar said the army lacks a clear political vision and is associated with coercion and abuses, leaving open whether the region is stabilizing or heading toward insurgency.

stories.headline: Global Microsoft Outage Disrupts Email, Teams and Copilot for Hundreds of Millions of Users
stories.summary:
A major outage hit Microsoft 365 services on Thursday evening, disrupting Outlook, Teams and the Copilot AI assistant. Many customers could not send or receive email, view files or access calendar details, while some users could still use Teams messaging and meetings. Downdetector logged about 140,000 reports of Outlook problems from 74 countries, though the true number is likely far higher because the site relies on self-reporting. Microsoft says more than 430 million people use its 365 apps.

Microsoft ruled out a cyber-security incident and attributed the disruption to "elevated load" on its infrastructure. A large number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable," it said, which pushed extra traffic onto the remaining servers and strained them. The company acknowledged that its early repair attempts were "not taking as expected."

The effects spread beyond the company's own products. OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems linked to the outage, and OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft services. The Singaporean government and Australia's spy agency said they were affected. In the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police forces and schools reported disruption, with some surgeries asking patients not to submit online messages and police urging the public to phone in reports.

On Friday morning Microsoft reported "early signs of stabilisation," but said service capacity had not yet returned to normal levels. The disruption continued into Asia-Pacific business hours. Cyber-security expert Troy Hunt said the episode shows how central Microsoft and email are to the internet's backbone, affecting work, appointments and account verification.

stories.headline: Update: Democrats Move Toward Congressional Majorities as Remaining House Races Are Called
stories.summary:
Democrats, who won the House and then the Senate in the midterm elections, are now settling the final races and preparing to govern. Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher was projected the winner of Kansas' governor's race over Trump-backed Republican Ty Masterson. In California's 4th District, Decision Desk HQ projected Eric Jones the winner over fellow Democrat Rep. Mike Thompson. In Alaska, a judge rejected Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola's request for rejected-ballot records as her narrow lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan shrank.

Republicans are absorbing the loss. Rep. Chip Roy of Texas gave a nearly half-hour rebuke of his party, and Jim Jordan won the House GOP minority leader race over Steve Scalise, 106-73. Former Vice President Mike Pence disputed JD Vance's claim that the Iran war alone cost Republicans Congress, citing inflation and policy failures as well. Trump, in an interview with Stephen A. Smith, was described as immovable in refusing to accept blame for the losses.

Democrats face their own tensions. Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced a challenge to Chuck Schumer for majority leader, and protesters from the Sunrise Movement were arrested in a sit-in at Schumer's office. Several senators, including Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin, reportedly oppose Schumer's bid. Meanwhile, Democrats say they plan investigations and hearings in January.

The White House has warned that Democratic oversight plans could amount to criminality, while Democrats argue oversight is a core congressional duty. Newly elected senators are in Washington for orientation, and Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico urged his party to deliver results quickly. The lame-duck Congress has about four weeks of scheduled work, with a government funding deadline approaching.

stories.headline: Update: Iran War Enters Ninth Month as Trump Says US Does Not Need a Deal
stories.summary:
The US-Israel war with Iran, which began with Trump's announcement of major combat operations on Feb. 28, continues with no clear exit strategy. BBC analysis said none of the choices facing Iran's leaders offers a clear path to victory after renewed strikes this week. Trump has repeatedly raised the prospect of renewing strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities, and satellite imagery from November appears to show digging and new buildings at such sites.

On Thursday Trump posted that the US does not need a deal with Iran, and redirected Vice President JD Vance, who had led efforts to restart negotiations, toward alleged corruption in Democratic-run cities and states. Axios reported that Vance had concluded the war drove Republicans' midterm losses. Oil prices rose and stocks fell after the post. Iran extended its shutout of UN nuclear inspectors, leaving the status of its uranium stockpile unknown, and an adviser to Iran's supreme leader said the US and Europe have heard the repercussions of the war.

The conflict is also affecting security at home and shipping abroad. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is among several administration officials living on military bases over safety concerns. BBC Verify found 12 vessels were struck in a week. Some Senate Democrats want to use the looming government funding deadline to force an end to the war, though party leaders have not decided whether to risk a shutdown. Republican supporters of the president's approach argue that pressure on Tehran is necessary, while critics in both parties question the war's costs and goals.

stories.headline: Update: Nvidia Scandal Pulls Commerce Secretary Lutnick Into Congressional Scrutiny
stories.summary:
Fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO has moved to Washington, where Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces scrutiny over whether his department did enough to keep advanced AI chips out of China. Critics say the department delayed adding the firm Megaspeed to a trade blacklist and shielded Nvidia as concerns grew over chip sales. The White House says it is standing by Lutnick, though reports describe a view inside the administration that he delayed action, and some reports say he could be fired.

Congressional responses cut across party lines. Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, a Republican, asked Lutnick and Huang to testify. Democrats Ron Wyden and Rep. Richard Neal asked Commerce to preserve records on Trump's decision to allow H200 chip sales to China. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries demanded a classified briefing for all members, and Democrats say Lutnick could face impeachment efforts or hearings in January.

Huang resigned Thursday after admitting an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese agent, amid reports of other relationships. The New York Times reported Trump called Huang on Tuesday and urged him to fight for his job, and Trump later called him "a Legend" while suggesting Tim Cook as a replacement. Because Nvidia chips underpin the global AI economy, analysts expect closer scrutiny of export controls. Some Democrats said the scandal shows lax oversight, while administration allies have defended the president's handling of chip policy.
